messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Housekeeper
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 44

**Patient Vignette: "David"**

David is a 25-year-old man who presents as quiet and watchful, his posture slightly hunched as if he’s trying to take up less space in the room. He works as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel, a job he has held for three years. He describes it as "good work" because it keeps his hands busy and his mind elsewhere. He is single and lives alone in a small studio apartment. He came to therapy at the urging of his supervisor, who noticed he had begun flinching violently when coworkers approached him from behind.

The story David tells begins in a small, tidy house in a suburb. He was the youngest of three children. His father was a truck driver, often gone for weeks at a time. His mother, a homemaker, was the center of his world until he was about six years old. That was when the rules changed. He recalls that his mother began to use a wooden spoon—not for cooking, but for correction. "I was a clumsy kid," he says, his voice flat. "I spilled milk. I left my shoes in the hall. I talked too much." The spoon was for talking too much. Later, it was her hand. Later still, it was whatever was nearby—a belt, a shoe, a hairbrush.

The logic of the abuse was always the same: she was teaching him discipline. She would tell him, "This hurts me more than it hurts you," as she struck his thighs and back, places the schoolteachers wouldn't see. He learned to stand still. He learned not to cry. If he cried, it meant he was being manipulative, and the punishment would start over. By the time he was ten, he had learned to dissociate completely. He would stare at a crack in the wall or a pattern in the linoleum and leave his body behind. He remembers the sensation of floating near the ceiling, looking down at a small boy being hit, and feeling nothing but a vague curiosity.

His father was rarely home, and when he was, he seemed not to notice. David never told him. He never told anyone. He believed, deeply and without question, that he deserved it. He was bad. He was clumsy. He talked too much.

The abuse stopped when he was fifteen. He had grown taller than his mother, and one day, when she raised her hand, he simply caught her wrist. He held it for a moment, looked at her, and then let go. He walked out of the house and didn't come back until the next morning. She never hit him again, but they never spoke of it either. The silence was its own kind of violence.

Now, ten years later, David lives in a world shaped by those years. He describes his daily life as a series of careful calculations. At the hotel, he cleans rooms on a strict schedule. He prefers the rooms of guests who have already checked out, so he can work alone. He cannot tolerate being watched. If a guest stays in the room while he cleans, his hands begin to shake. He apologizes constantly—for bumping a chair, for the sound of the vacuum, for existing. His coworkers have learned not to touch him. One well-meaning woman placed a hand on his shoulder to thank him, and he dropped a stack of clean towels and backed into a corner, his heart pounding so hard he thought he was having a heart attack. He avoids the break room. He eats lunch in his car.

At home, he keeps his apartment immaculate—a mirror of his work life. He says he cannot relax in a messy space. He sleeps on the far edge of his bed, closest to the door. He sleeps lightly, waking at any sound. He has nightmares, though he calls them "bad dreams." He dreams of being small and trapped, of a door that won't open, of a voice that says, "This is for your own good."

He has never had a romantic relationship. He finds the idea of intimacy terrifying. "I don't know how to let anyone close," he says, looking at his hands. "I don't know how to be touched without flinching." He has few friends. He says he prefers it that way. He has learned that people eventually disappoint or hurt you, and it's easier to be alone.

Despite these struggles, David has never missed a day of work. He is reliable, meticulous, and invisible. He prides himself on not being a problem. He is not angry. He does not drink. He has never been in a fight. He simply moves through the world as if he is trying not to be seen, trying not to take up space, trying not to be a burden. He says, with a hollow laugh, "I guess I learned my lesson well."
